title: Oil Prices Slide as Global Glut Fears Eclipse Hormuz Attacks | OilPrice.com

Crude oil prices extended a decline that began earlier this month, as reports about a global glut multiplied, suggesting there was no supply squeeze at all, despite continuing attacks on vessels in the Persian Gulf and the Yemeni Houthis’ strikes on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $91.70 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate was trading at $85.03 per barrel, both down from Monday’s close.

The price decline came in spite of reports about tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, evidence that shipping in the waterway is still far from safe, especially when it comes to oil. For days, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents with tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as “unauthorized” in the Strait of Hormuz.

Moreover, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy warned oil tanker and oil firm owners that “the U.S.-backed southern passage through the strait had been mined, cautioning that trusting U.S. military officials and cooperating with them would put their vessels at risk.”

Yet traders appear focused exclusively on reports about the rebound in Middle Eastern oil exports, even as data from Windward suggests overall traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remains severely subdued, compared to pre-war daily averages.

“Oil is recalibrating lower as the market increasingly accepts that supply has finally caught up with demand and may now be set to exceed it. That shift in the supply-demand balance is the main factor weighing on prices today,” Reuters quoted KCM Trade’s chief economist Tim Waterer as saying.

The expectation of supply exceeding demand came from the International Energy Agency and two investment banks, which estimated that demand destruction has been more serious than the supply squeeze and will outlast it, with the glut manifesting this quarter and extending into next year, according to the IEA.
